query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the element X determines the nature of the high‐temperature oxide scale. When X is Al or Si, selective oxidation leads to the formation of a slow-growing, dense, and coherent oxide (Al2O3 or SiO2) that adheres well to the substrate and acts as a protective barrier above 900 °C. In contrast, when X is Mn, the resulting oxide scale forms more rapidly as a loosely adherent, non-coherent spinel or mixed oxide which is prone to cracking and spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, with X alloyed as either Al, Si, or Mn.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C for an extended duration.
generation.conditions: High-temperature (≥900 °C) oxidation/corrosion testing in controlled atmospheric conditions (e.g., dry air or simulated service environment) that allows in situ assessment of oxide formation.
generation.structural_mediator: The integrity and phase coherence of the surface oxide layer (e.g., formation of slow-growing, adherent Al2O3 or SiO2 versus fast-growing Mn-rich oxides or spinels) mediate the protective behavior.
generation.mechanism: Selective oxidation of the X element governs the oxide formation kinetics and adherence: Al and Si form thermodynamically stable, high-melting oxides with low diffusivity that grow slowly and maintain structural integrity due to good compatibility with the substrate, whereas Mn oxidizes to form more rapidly growing, non-coherent oxides that do not bond well, leading to scale cracking and spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with X = Al or Si will develop a thin, continuous, and adherent oxide layer that grows slowly and does not crack or spall under prolonged exposure above 900 °C, while alloys with X = Mn will show thicker, less uniform oxide scales prone to cracking and spallation.
generation.baseline: The baseline is represented by the CrFeCoNiMn alloy, which prior evidence indicates produces non-protective, quickly degrading oxide scales.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to high-entropy alloys in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, exposed to oxidative/corrosive atmospheres at temperatures at or above 900 °C for durations sufficient to observe oxidation kinetics and scale integrity.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative differences in oxide growth rate and critical thickness thresholds are not well-defined and may depend on additional alloying interactions and processing conditions. The influence of possible multiphase distributions on oxidation behavior also remains to be further clarified.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of CrFeCoNiX alloys with X precisely controlled as Al, Si, or Mn under identical processing conditions to achieve comparable single- or multiphase microstructures. Expose these samples in a controlled oxidation furnace at ≥900 °C in a simulated service atmosphere. Monitor the oxide layer formation in situ (e.g., via high-temperature X-ray diffraction) and conduct post-exposure microstructural and adhesion analyses (using SEM, TEM, and adhesion tests).
measurements: Oxide phase identity and coherence (via XRD and electron microscopy)
Adhesion quality and presence of scale cracking/spallation
Elemental distribution across the oxide-metal interface (using EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If alloys with X = Al or Si do not show a statistically significant slower oxide growth rate and improved adhesion compared to the Mn alloy (i.e., if the oxide morphology, thickness, and adherence are essentially equivalent across different X elements), or if the Al/Si-containing alloys also exhibit premature cracking/spallation, then the hypothesis that the nature of X controls the formation of a protective, coherent oxide layer is falsified.

## Abstract
This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr2O3, Fe2O3, or Fe3O4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. ## Abstract
AbstractAs protective coatings for the thermal parts of aero-engines, AlCoCrFeNi coatings have good application prospects. In this study, atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) was used to prepare AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy coatings (HECs), which were oxidized from 650 °C to 1000 °C. The mechanism of the oxide layer formation and the internal phase transition were systematically investigated. The results show that a mixed oxide scale with a laminated structure was formed at the initial stage of oxidation. The redistribution of elements and phase transition occurred in the HECs’ matrix; the BCC/B2 structure transformed to Al-Ni ordered B2 phase and Fe-Cr disordered A2 phase.Keywords: plasma spraying, oxidation behavior, high-entropy coatings, phase transition
